title: Regina transit lockout ends after tentative deal reached
summary: The transit worker lockout is over in Regina after the city and Amalgamated Transit Union (ATU) Local 588 reached a tentative three-year agreement late Monday evening.

image.caption: Regina transit workers picketed outside the Transit Operations Centre on Monday after getting locked out by the city. (Alex Kozroski)

blocks.text: The transit worker lockout is over in Regina after the city and Amalgamated Transit Union (ATU) Local 588 reached a tentative three-year agreement late Monday evening.
Regular bus service expected to resume Tuesday afternoon
The transit worker lockout is over in Regina after the city and Amalgamated Transit Union (ATU) Local 588 reached a tentative agreement late Monday evening.
"Along with the tentative three-year deal, the two sides agreed to end the lockout and the union's voluntary overtime ban," the City of Regina said in a news release shortly after.
"The city recognizes the significant impact the labour disruption has had on transit riders, employees and the broader Regina community and thanks residents for their patience and understanding. "

The city noted that regular transit service would not be ready for the Tuesday morning commute, but that the city is focused on "reinstating that service safely and efficiently" as early as Tuesday afternoon.
The agreement brings an end to the one-day lockout, which paused regular bus service.

After two years without a contract, ATU Local 588 leadership directed its 380 members on Friday to no longer take voluntary overtime shifts. In response, Regina's director of transit operations sent city employees a letter on Saturday advising them that only management and security personnel would be allowed to access Regina Transit facilities, yards and depots effective Monday at 3 a.m. CST.
The lockout formally began on Monday at 11 a.m. CST.
The two sides returned to the bargaining table later that day with the assistance of a provincial mediator.
“It’s been a long fight for our members for the past two years without a contract, but we have stood strong and united,” Local 588 vice-president Pat Nichol said in a news release late Monday night.

“This lockout made us even more resolute. Our new contract will not only give our members a living wage and other improvements, but it also ensures a reliable transit system for our riders and community.”
While most details of the tentative deal have yet to be released, the union said it includes wage increases.
